1. In 1996 a unique experiment was carried out with the Hubble Space Telescope: it was required to see the faintest possible objects in the sky, unreachable by ground-based equipment. As a result of many-hour exposures taken with four colour filters, images were obtained of a small area of the sky far from the Milky Way with an area of several square arcminutes, where objects down to magnitude 29–30 can be distinguished. You are given photocopies of the images (obtained with some reduction of the limiting magnitude). On the original images about 2000 galaxies were found, but only for a small part of them can the morphological type be determined with confidence. Your task: for selected objects (they are marked with numbers), determine (by their appearance and colour shade) to which class they belong. Use the notation:

• * – a star of our Galaxy
• S – spiral galaxy
• E – elliptical galaxy
• Ir – irregular galaxy

Where the subclass of the galaxy can be indicated, indicate it: type Sa or Sc.

Note: galaxy No. 30 is not indicated quite accurately: you will find it by moving the arrow 30° anticlockwise.

2. On 1 January 1998 the government of the galaxy "Milky Way" carried out a 1:1000 denomination of "measures and weights" within the galaxy. The denomination extends over a region of the Universe of (initial) radius 20 kpc centred on the centre of our Galaxy. The centre of the galaxy remains in the same place relative to other galaxies, the spatial orientation does not change, but all distances between objects within the galaxy decrease by a factor of 1000. In the same region the mass of all matter is denominated, that is, the masses of all macro- and micro-objects, even elementary particles and electromagnetic waves, decrease by a factor of 1000. In addition, throughout 1998 the "old" values of all world constants (the speed of light, the gravitational constant, Planck's constant, etc.) remain in force.

Investigate the consequences of the denomination for the population of the galaxy. In particular, to what physical consequences will this lead in 1998, will the galaxy and its objects be stable, what will astronomer-scientists discover, etc. And, if the government of the galaxy has decided on a denomination of "measures and weights", what other physical parameters would it be worth denominating as well?

The singularity and the violation of some conservation laws at the moment of the sharp denomination on 1 January are not to be considered.

1. On the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram the band of the main sequence has a rather noticeable width. One of the reasons for this is the presence of binary stars not resolved into separate components. What is the spread in luminosity (in stellar magnitudes) for stars of the same spectral class that may be associated with this effect?

3. A spacecraft revolves around a certain planet in a circular orbit of radius $R_0 = 10000$ km with an orbital speed $V_o = 12$ km/s. At some moment the speed of the craft was increased by $\Delta V = 3$ km/s without changing its direction.

a) What did the periapsis and apoapsis of the orbit of the craft become after this?

b) What is the speed of the craft at apoapsis?

c) Find the mass of the planet.

In their apparent motion across the sky, planets pass through so-called stationary points, where they change the direction of their motion along the ecliptic: from direct to retrograde or vice versa. Take, for example, Mercury. How are the moments of its stationary points related to the moments of its greatest eastern and western elongations (angular distances from the Sun)? Choose the correct answer and justify it; it is desirable to accompany the justification with a drawing:

1. They coincide with them.
2. They immediately precede them.
3. They occur immediately after them.
4. They occur after the eastern and before the western.
5. They occur after the western and before the eastern.
6. They occur twice per synodic period of the planet, independently of the maximum elongations.
7. They occur at the conjunctions (superior and inferior).
8. For Mercury this reasoning makes no sense, since only the outer planets change their motion from direct to retrograde.

Observations of a radio galaxy at a distance of a billion light years from us showed that an ejection of a compact radio source occurred from the nucleus of the galaxy, which in one year moved away from the nucleus by a distance of about $10^{-3}$ arcsecond. If we assume that the radio source moves rectilinearly with a speed close to the speed of light ($c = 300\,000$ km/s), then at what angle to the line of sight did the ejection occur?

6. Can the Moon be seen from the surface of Mars with the naked eye? The stellar magnitude of the Moon at full moon as seen from the Earth is $-12.8^m$, the mean distance from the Earth to the Moon is 384 thousand km, from the Sun to Mars 1.52 au. Confirm your answer by calculation; in particular, estimate the stellar magnitude of the Moon visible from Mars in the case when the Earth is, for the Martians, at its greatest eastern elongation.

7. Despite last year's unsuccessful experiment with the denomination of measures and weights, and the insistent requests of the participants of the V Russian Astronomy Olympiad not to experiment like this any more, the government of the galaxy "Milky Way" continued last year to change the parameters of its galaxy. The central photon bank of the galaxy overestimated its abilities and carried out an emission not backed by a sufficient amount of photon energy. The photons were issued of the same colour as before and of the same mass, but their number in space increased sharply. As a result of such uncontrolled emission a so-called "photon inflation" occurred, and by the end of the year the exchange rate of the light year with respect to the parsec had fallen sharply: 1 parsec was no longer 3.26 light years, as before, but as many as 14 light years. Considering that the parsec is a stable quantity, not subject to inflation (after all, it is determined only from geometric considerations), describe what happened in the galaxy as a result of such "photon inflation". Which physical constants changed, and in which direction? What can the astronomers of our Galaxy now learn about the Universe to a greater (and also to a lesser) extent (at present, in the near and distant future)? What will the galaxy "Milky Way" look like for the astronomers of other galaxies? And what would you advise the government of the galaxy "Milky Way" to undertake in order to stabilise the situation and return the ratio familiar from childhood, 3.26 light years = 1 parsec?

So our whole planet receives more solar energy than it would receive without refraction. Where, then, does the additional energy come from?

A civilization of "little green men" living on one of the planets orbiting that star has also become interested in our Sun. 5. An eclipsing binary star has been discovered. The size of the second star is negligibly small compared with the size of the first. It is known that the major axes of the orbits of the stars lie along the line of sight. The duration of the eclipse of the second component by the first and of the passage of the second component across the disk of the first are respectively $T_1 = 8{,}7$ hours and $T_2 = 11{,}3$ hours, with an orbital period $T = 17$ days. 6. Two stars have the same mass, the same density and the same pressure at the centre. However, in one of the stars the core consists of the normal mixture of ionized hydrogen and helium (the number of helium atoms is about 10 times smaller than the number of hydrogen atoms), while in the second it consists entirely of fully ionized carbon. If the temperature in the core of the first star is $2\cdot10^{7}$ K, what is it in the core of the second star?

Treat the gas as ideal. Number of protons in the nuclei of the atoms: $H$ – 1, $He$ – 2, $C$ – 6. Atomic weights of the nuclei: $A_H = 1$, $A_{He} = 4$, $A_C = 12$.

7. "Ageing of photons" (creative problem).

You must know that in the spectra of distant galaxies a red shift is observed, and the farther the galaxy is from us, the larger the shift. At present this is explained within the model of the expanding Universe, according to which the galaxies recede from us with relative velocity $V = HR$ (where $H = 75$ km/s / Mpc is the Hubble constant and $R$ is the distance to the galaxy), and the red shift is the result of the Doppler effect associated with this velocity.

However, some time ago the hypothesis was widespread that the red shift in the spectra of distant galaxies is due not to the Doppler effect but to the "ageing of photons". The idea of this hypothesis is that with time photons lose their energy (that is, their energy decreases according to the law $E = E_0\cdot e^{-t/T}$, where $t$ is the lifetime of the photon and $T$ is some constant). Thus it simply turns out that light from distant galaxies travels for a very long time, during which the photons lose part of their energy, i.e. "redden".

Consider a hypothetical situation: suppose photons really do age, and age 1000 times faster than follows from our observations (that is, $\Delta E/At$ is 1000 times larger than for us). In particular, consider such questions: What theories of the evolution of the Universe could exist in this case? What would change in the theory of the expanding Universe? Would scientists guess that it is precisely the ageing of photons that exists? And so on.

Bear in mind that modern instruments measuring radial velocities by the Doppler effect record these velocities with an accuracy of up to a few metres per second (say, 3 m/s).

8. "The stellar wind of P Cygni" (practical problem). This task is dedicated to the 400th anniversary of the discovery of the most famous of the stars that actively lose matter.

On 18 August 1600 the Dutch cartographer and mathematician Willem Blaeu (the very one who wrote the "Cosmography" from which Peter I studied) discovered a new star in Cygnus. In the 17th century its brightness twice rose to 3rd magnitude and fell to 6th–7th, but since the beginning of the 18th century it has changed little and still remains close to 5th magnitude. In 1886 Pickering drew attention to the unusual spectrum of P Cygni.

Before you is a small part of it with four lines of ionized nitrogen, and the same part taken from the spectrum of HD 190603 – a star close to P Cygni in temperature and luminosity. Both spectra were obtained with the spectrograph at the coudé focus of the 1-m telescope of the SAO RAS. In the spectra of most stars (including HD 190603) absorption lines are observed (in them the intensity of the radiation is below the level of the radiation in the continuous spectrum), while in the spectra of nebulae and of some stars with extended envelopes there are emission lines. In the spectrum of P Cygni almost all lines are absorption-emission lines. Their profiles are called "P Cygni-type profiles".

а) Using the attached simplest scheme of an expanding envelope (stellar wind), explain the specific shape of the "P Cygni-type profiles". Mark with the appropriate letters the parts of the profile formed in the corresponding parts of the envelope.

б) From the attached fragment of the spectrum, estimate the velocity of the stellar wind of P Cygni. The wavelength scale (in ångströms) is given for a source at rest. Each of the divisions on the left corresponds to 1 Å.
